g.text: Shard by the key your hottest query is scoped to - not by a hash chosen for even spread
Every constraint and index here traces back to one requirement: one dead subscriber must never slow down another.
which is why a delivery is scoped to a
ONE durable, immutable copy of the event,
stored once regardless of how many
APPEND-ONLY: one row per HTTP attempt,
An event matching 5 subscriptions produces 5 deliveries rows - and storing the
payload on each one would multiply storage by the FAN-OUT FACTOR for no benefit,
since all 5 are delivering the IDENTICAL bytes. So deliveries references
ingested_events.id instead: one write, N reads, and a single place to look up
'what did we actually send' for an audit or a dead-letter replay - rather than
dead_lettered is a VALUE deliveries.status can take, not a separate table - and the
reason is what has to be true for a replay. A job scheduler's dead-lettered
outbox row has nothing further to reference; a dead-lettered DELIVERY still needs
its subscription, its event and its full attempt history intact and joinable
exactly as they were. Moving it would mean either copying all of that across or
leaving the real table pointing a foreign key into a second location, for no
query that actually benefits from the split.
Two unique constraints, each carrying a whole guarantee
The fan-out step's actual concurrency-safety mechanism - the same role an
idempotency_key's unique index plays in payments. Re-consuming the same bus
message (a producer's own at-least-once redelivery, or the ingestion consumer's
crash-and-resume) attempts to insert the same pairs a second time, and the
constraint turns that into a CHEAP NO-OP INSERT FAILURE instead of a duplicate
delivery being fanned out and eventually double-sent to a real endpoint.
The ordering guarantee's actual enforcement point. sequence_number is assigned
monotonically PER SUBSCRIPTION at fan-out time, and the claim query's NOT EXISTS
gate checks the IMMEDIATELY PRECEDING number for the same subscription - a query
that is only fast, and only correct against concurrent writers, because this
composite index turns 'is sequence N-1 for this subscriber still pending' into a
single indexed row lookup rather than a scan. It also prevents two rows ever
claiming the same position in one subscriber's queue.
deliveries(status, next_attempt_at) the claim query's core predicate - 'what is due for an attempt right now' -
and the single most important index in this schema, playing the same role as
deliveries(subscription_id, sequence_number) UNIQUE: both the ordering gate's lookup path and the mechanism preventing two
deliveries(event_id, subscription_id) UNIQUE: the idempotent-fan-out mechanism above
delivery_attempts(delivery_id, attempt_number) the dead-letter dashboard's 'full attempt history for this delivery, in
event_subscriptions(tenant_id, event_type, the fan-out writer's 'which active subscriptions match this event' query,
status) run once per ingested event
Consistency - two tables where a stale read is a subscriber-visible bug
a rotated secret or an updated endpoint URL must be visible to the VERY NEXT delivery attempt, not eventually. A stale read
here is not cosmetic - it is signature verification failing against a secret that was supposed to be revoked, or a delivery
still hitting a URL the customer just disabled.
STRONGLY CONSISTENT for the claim and the gate
the same non-negotiable bar the job scheduler sets for its due-jobs claim: a stale read of 'is the prior sequence terminal' is
exactly the gap that lets two attempts for one subscriber run OUT OF ORDER.
append-only; a replica is a legitimate fit
for the dead-letter dashboard's historical queries - the same way payments' ledger entries and the scheduler's job runs both
tolerate replica lag on reporting paths. A replica lagging a few seconds does not change what already happened, only how
promptly a dashboard reflects the very latest attempt.
for the rare dead-letter-replay payload fetch. A replica is fine here for the same reason.
Three tables, three different scaling axes
this keeps one subscriber's ENTIRE ordered queue on a
single shard, so the sequence gate's 'is the prior
sequence terminal' check is always a single-shard lookup -
never a cross-shard fan-out-and-merge. The same principle
as payments' account-scoped ledger sharding and the
bounded by the number of registered ENDPOINTS, which grows
far slower than delivery volume - so it can stay unsharded
(or shard by tenant_id independently) far longer than
ingested_events -> by raw event volume, not fan-out
deliveries outgrows ingested_events by roughly the ~1.6x
average fan-out factor - the same way a double-entry
ledger outgrows payment intents 2:1. Different systems,
same shape of reason to scale two tables independently
rather than assume one scheme fits both.
Trace the three modules together: 'one dead subscriber must never slow down another' is why the design fans out into one
(event, subscription) row per match instead of resolving subscriptions at delivery time; that same requirement is why
(subscription_id, sequence_number) exists here as a unique, indexed pair rather than an afterthought column - it is the
concrete mechanism that makes the ordering gate a single fast lookup instead of a scan. And sharding deliveries by
subscription_id, not by an event id or a hash, is what keeps that same lookup fast past billions of rows.
